Students assume each grid line on a bar graph represents one unit, leading to incorrect totals.
Students believe a trapezium must have two pairs of parallel sides or equal non-parallel sides.
Students count lines of symmetry by guessing based on visual balance rather than testing reflectional equivalence.
Students assume all angles in an isosceles triangle are equal or confuse the exterior angle with a base angle when finding x on a straight line.
Students calculate the number of diagonals in a hexagon as n-3 (6) or n(n-3) (18) instead of using the correct formula.
Students assume angles on a straight line are always equal (90° each) rather than supplementary.
The sequence '3, 1, 4, 2, 5' dictates the required order for analyzing or matching figures.
Figures are related by surface-level visual similarity rather than a consistent geometric or logical transformation.
Each figure in the first group corresponds directly to a figure in the second group by its original position or index.
Students interpret 'by Preeti' as indicating physical location or ownership rather than authorship.
Students assume 'is A.' describes a literal shape, grade, or physical attribute of the basket.
Students expect mathematical operations due to the word 'basket' triggering quantitative schemas instead of textual analysis.
Whole numbers and natural numbers are identical sets.
Every whole number has a predecessor within the set of whole numbers.
Every whole number is strictly greater than zero.
Students believe that adding a fixed amount to both length and breadth preserves the rectangle's original proportions.
Students think enlargement refers exclusively to an increase in perimeter rather than area.
Students assume that increasing length and breadth by the same numerical value results in a proportionally larger rectangle.
A chord is an infinite line that passes through two points on a circle.
All chords must pass through the center of the circle.
A chord can connect any two points located inside or on the boundary of a circle.
